measures: Status: stat (guidance). NWS 'JetStream' training page: 'Divide the number of seconds by five to get the distance the lightning is away from you' and 'Do not resume outdoor activities until 30 minutes after the last thunder clap.' The NWS thunder page (https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-science-thunder) gives 5 seconds = 1 mile, 15 seconds = 3 miles, and says thunder 'can be heard for a distance of only about 10 miles from the lightning strike'. A vendor paper warns the count has limits: thunder may not be heard in wind or rough terrain and can be matched to the wrong flash (https://www.vaisala.com/sites/default/files/documents/1.Leick-How%20Lightning.pdf, PDF p.5).
source_title: NWS JetStream - Lightning Safety
publisher: NOAA National Weather Service (JetStream training page)
quote: If lightning is seen and the time delay to its subsequent thunder is 30 seconds or less
use_in_story: Animate a flash, a counter and a circle that grows one mile every five seconds, to show why a sensor reading beats a human count.

topic: Construction stop-work rule: lifts, scaffold, roofing and open-area work stop; 10 miles and 30 minutes (US Army Corps of Engineers manual)
figure: 10 miles; resume 30 minutes after the last thunder or lightning
measures: Status: stat (rule quoted second hand). The page prints paragraph (4) under 'Emergency Planning Section 01.E.01' of the US Army Corps of Engineers Safety and Health Requirements Manual EM 385-1-1. In the same paragraph, when lightning is observed all load handling equipment (cranes and lifts), drill rigs, work on elevated platforms or scaffolding, roofing, tree trimming, pole climbing and work in open areas must stop, and someone must judge how close the lightning is to the work. It also gives the divide-by-5 count. The page does not print an edition date, and the USACE host could not be reached from the fetch tool, so the primary text was not read. A vendor paper says the National Lightning Safety Institute advises construction workers to be aware when lightning is 20-40 miles from the site and to suspend work and evacuate when it is within 10 miles (https://www.vaisala.com/sites/default/files/documents/1.Leick-How%20Lightning.pdf, PDF p.3). The same paper rates construction lightning risk 'High' and safety-tool adoption 'Low'.
year: Edition not printed on the page

publisher: OSHAcademy (quoting US Army Corps of Engineers EM 385-1-1)

use_in_story: Draw a 10-mile ring around a site that flips lifts, drill rigs, scaffold, roofing and open-area work to Stop and starts the 30-minute clock.

topic: Typical alert radii used by authorities and industries
figure: 5 nautical miles (roughly 6 statute miles or 9.26 km) for sports; NCAA 8 miles; airports 10 and 5 miles; wind farms 50 and 30 miles; WMO stations 8 km and 8-16 km
measures: Status: stat (guidance, mixed sources). Primary: the athletic trainers' position statement (J Athl Train 2013;48(2):258-270, PDF p.3, recommendations 15 and 17) says everyone must be fully inside a safe place when the edge of the lightning storm reaches 5 nautical miles, and activity stays suspended until 30 minutes after the last strike seen within 5 nautical miles. Sydney 2000 Olympics used three stages: yellow 60 minutes from the storm, orange 30 minutes, red when lightning is within 10 km (PDF p.9). Other documents: NCAA 8-mile radius with a 30-minute all-clear, and wind farms notify at 50 miles, stop work at 30 miles with a 15-minute all-clear (vendor paper, 2010, https://www.vaisala.com/sites/default/files/documents/1.Leick-How%20Lightning.pdf, PDF p.3-4); Denver airport advisory at 10 miles, warning at 5 miles, secure after 15 minutes with none within 5 miles, and 5-mile and 3-mile limits recommended by airline trade bodies (ACRP Report 8, https://www.idc-online.com/technical_references/pdfs/electrical_engineering/acrp_rpt_008.pdf, PDF p.36-37); WMO reports a thunderstorm at an automated station for lightning within 8 kilometres and 'in the vicinity' at 8 to 16 km (WMO-No. 1198, https://amc.namem.gov.mn/wp-content/uploads/WMO/21.%201198_en.pdf?_t=1638837870, PDF p.15). The vendor paper's rule of thumb: start at 6 miles and add 1 mile for each 2 minutes of evacuation time.
region: United States (sports, airports, wind farms), Australia (Sydney 2000), WMO (global)
source_title: National Athletic Trainers' Association Position Statement: Lightning Safety for Athletics and Recreation
publisher: Journal of Athletic Training (National Athletic Trainers' Association)
quote: reaches 5 nautical miles (nmi; roughly 6 statute miles or 9.26 km
use_in_story: Show nested rings for alert, warning and stop, and let each industry's ring size differ, so the platform needs a per-site setting.

topic: Downtime and cost of a strict 30/30 lightning rule (airport ramps, modeled)

topic: NOAA-linked lightning nowcast: how many minutes of warning
figure: Median lead time 17.5 min to the first lightning flash; 'frequently ... 20 min or more'; a quarter of hits 32.5 min or more; 0-60-min forecast window
measures: Status: stat (published verification, satellite model). LightningCast by scientists at NOAA/NESDIS and the University of Wisconsin (CIMSS), trained on GOES satellite images. Test: GOES-16 CONUS scenes, the 5th to 9th of each month of 2020, points about every 80 km. With the lightning-onset criterion the median lead time to the first flash is 17.5 min at the 30% and 40% probability thresholds (12.5 min without the criterion), and a quarter of true-positive predictions measured 32.5 min or more (PDF p.13, journal p.1251). The output is a probability for the next 60 minutes, not a certainty. CIMSS blog, 31 January 2025: version 2 'will be operational at NOAA later in 2025' (https://cimss.ssec.wisc.edu/satellite-blog/archives/62924). WMO defines nowcasting as 'from the present to 6 hours ahead' (WMO-No. 1198, PDF p.11) and says lightning detection systems 'increase warning lead times for dangerous thunderstorms' without giving a minute figure (PDF p.19).
region: United States (CONUS test); model also runs on GOES full disk
source_title: ProbSevere LightningCast: A Deep-Learning Model for Satellite-Based Lightning Nowcasting
publisher: Weather and Forecasting 37(7), 1239-1257 (American Meteorological Society); NOAA repository copy
quote: LightningCast, which frequently provides 20 min or more of lead time to new lightning activity
use_in_story: Show a probability bar rising ahead of the first strike with a bracket of about 17 to 20 minutes, which is the time a work plan has to pause lifts.

topic: No system can predict the first lightning strike
figure: None: no system can detect the first strike, detect all lightning, or predict strikes (NOAA and OSHA)
measures: Status: stat (official caution). The fact sheet says commercial detection and notification services can send alerts when lightning develops or moves within a set range of a work site, but cannot predict the first strike, so workers must watch the sky and reach shelter before the first strike. NOAA recommends employers first rely on NOAA weather reports. Handheld detectors are described as less accurate than commercial networks. PDF p.3.

publisher: US Department of Labor, OSHA, with NOAA
quote: no systems can detect the "first strike," detect all lightning, or predict lightning strikes.
use_in_story: Be honest on the slide: show lead time as a probability with a margin, and keep a human stop rule on top.

topic: Farm work in one year of global lightning news reports (2021), and the Gulf gap
figure: Farming named in 125 incidents, 185 deaths and 143 injuries; all reports: 505 incidents, 765 deaths, 560 injuries, 46 nations; no Gulf nation among them
measures: Status: stat (media-based sample, biased). The Indian subcontinent has 320 of the 505 incidents. Table IV (PDF p.3) lists no Saudi Arabia, UAE, Oman, Kuwait, Qatar or Bahrain; Israel and Turkey are listed under Europe. Absence in an English-news method is not proof of no incidents. Single-victim events are under-reported (only 42% of incidents involve one person, against 93% in the US). Caution: the paper also prints 'Farming accounts for 35% of the events', but 125 of 505 is 24.8% and 185 of 765 deaths is 24.2% (my arithmetic), so use the counts, not the 35%. Farm sentence is in section VII.

publisher: Conference paper hosted by the African Centres for Lightning and Electromagnetics Network (ACLENet)

topic: OSHA hazardous atmosphere: the oxygen band and 10 percent of the lower flammable limit
figure: Oxygen below 19.5 percent or above 23.5 percent; flammable gas, vapor, or mist in excess of 10 percent of its lower flammable limit (LFL)
measures: Status: stat (US federal rule text). Items (3) and (1) of the definition of 'Hazardous atmosphere' in 29 CFR 1910.146(b), for permit-required confined spaces. Cornell LII shows the same wording (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1910.146). The construction rule repeats both items in 29 CFR 1926.1202 (https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1926/1926.1202). Hot work in shipyards uses a different oxygen number: 29 CFR 1915.11 defines 'Safe for hot work' as oxygen content that 'does not exceed 22.0 percent by volume' and flammable vapors 'less than 10 percent of the lower explosive limit' (https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1915/1915.11). OSHA writes LFL in 1910.146 and LEL in 1915.11, and uses 10 percent in both. The hot work paragraphs read in 1926.352(i) and 1910.252(a)(3)(i) give no percent. They say containers must be cleaned, ventilated and tested.

topic: Confined-space permit: test order, recorded results, continuous monitoring and keeping the permit
figure: Test first for oxygen, then combustible gases and vapors, then toxic gases and vapors; permit records test results with tester names or initials and when tested; cancelled permits kept at least 1 year
measures: Status: stat (US federal rule text). 29 CFR 1910.146(d)(5)(iii) gives the test order. (c)(5)(ii)(C) also requires testing 'with a calibrated direct-reading instrument' before an employee enters. (d)(5)(i): where the space is large or part of a continuous system such as a sewer, entry conditions 'shall be continuously monitored in the areas where authorized entrants are working'. (f)(10): the permit lists the 'results of initial and periodic tests ... accompanied by the names or initials of the testers and by an indication of when the tests were performed'. (e)(6): 'retain each cancelled entry permit for at least 1 year'. Construction rule 29 CFR 1926.1204(e)(2) says 'Continuously monitor atmospheric hazards' unless continuous equipment is not commercially available or periodic monitoring is frequent enough; (e)(3) repeats the test order (https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1926/1926.1204, same text at https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1926.1204). NIOSH Alert 86-110 also says confined spaces 'should be tested prior to entry and continually monitored' (see S3-12).
source_title: 1910.146 Permit-required confined spaces, paragraphs (c)(5), (d)(5), (e)(6) and (f)(10)
publisher: US Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
quote: test first for oxygen, then for combustible gases and vapors, and then for toxic gases and vapors
use_in_story: Fill a permit card with three timed readings in order (oxygen, LEL, toxics) and stamp a 1 year retention tag on it, to show the permit is a record the data bank can hold.

topic: Hot work fire watch after the torch is off: OSHA half hour, NFPA 51B one hour
figure: OSHA: at least a half hour after welding or cutting; NFPA 51B 2019 edition: a minimum of 1 hour (section 5.6.1.1)
measures: Status: stat (rule text; NFPA through its committee record, not the standard itself). OSHA 29 CFR 1910.252(a)(2)(iii)(B): 'A fire watch shall be maintained for at least a half hour after completion of welding or cutting operations' (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1910.252, same wording on osha.gov). The NFPA committee file (public inputs and committee statements dated 2020 and 2021) says the example permit text 'was not changed to reflect the code change of a minimum of 1 hour in section 5.6.1.1' and the committee wrote 'There is a recognized need for a 1 hr fire watch'. The same file records that the CSB asked for monitoring to keep gas 'less than the LFL (generally less than 10% LFL)'. The committee says it offered a First Revision while allowing 'time for further review of NFPA 326'. So the numeric gas limit was not read inside NFPA 51B itself. Also from OSHA: 1910.252(a)(2)(iv) prefers 'a written permit' for hot work; 1910.119(k)(1) says 'The employer shall issue a hot work permit' for hot work on or near a covered process (https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.119); 1926.352(i) requires containers that held toxic or flammable substances to be cleaned, ventilated and 'tested' before welding or cutting (https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1926/1926.352). The PDF came back as binary through WebFetch, so the text was read with a local extractor.
year: NFPA 51B 2019 edition (committee file dated 2020 and 2021); OSHA text in force
source_title: NFPA 51B public inputs and committee statements, Technical Committee on Hot Work Operations (file 51B_A2023_HWO_AAA_FD_PIResponses.pdf)

topic: Hot work on tanks: over 60 deaths since 1990 and gas monitoring before and during the work

measures: Status: stat. US Chemical Safety Board Safety Bulletin No. 2009-01-SB, February 2010, introduction on PDF page 2. Page 11: in one refinery tank case gas was tested only at the start, 'five hours between the last gas test and the explosion', and the air warmed by 14 degrees. The bulletin gives no percent LEL number. The PDF came back as binary through WebFetch, so the text was read with a local extractor.

topic: Wind limit for lifting people by crane (OSHA)

Page 2 captions a crane photo 'Cranes are especially vulnerable to lightning.' Page 3: no systems can detect the first strike, detect all lightning, or predict lightning strikes. The emergency action plan should say when to suspend and when to resume outdoor work and the time needed to reach shelter. NWS adds that lightning can strike outward 10 miles from a thunderstorm so hearing thunder means you are likely within striking distance (https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-science-overview) and that lightning kills about 20 people a year in the US (https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-victims). NWS analysis for 2006 to 2019: 18% of 418 US lightning deaths were work-related, of which construction 21% and roofing 17% (https://www.weather.gov/media/safety/Analysis06-19.pdf, pages 1 and 8). topic: Permit-to-work failure in a major disaster (Piper Alpha, 1988)
figure: 167 men lost their lives; possible failings in the permit to work system were identified as an element in the disaster
measures: UK House of Commons Hansard, 12 November 1990, statement by the Secretary of State for Energy on the public inquiry report: sympathy for the 167 men who lost their lives, and his department's technical investigation identified possible failings in the operator's permit to work system. Hansard 7 March 1991 debate: 226 men were on the platform on the night of 6 July 1988 and only 61 of those men survived (https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1991/mar/07/piper-alpha-cullen-report). Do not say 167 of 226: the sources give the two figures separately. HSE guidance HSG250 (2005), PDF page 6, reminds readers of the importance of permit-to-work failures in the sequence of events leading to Piper Alpha; case study 4 (page 9) says there was no cross-referencing between permits and reliance was placed on memory; case study 12 (page 13) says handovers failed to communicate that PSV 504 (a pressure safety valve) had been removed for overhaul; case study 6 (page 10) says a 1989 vapour cloud explosion at a chemical complex in the USA killed 23 people and injured 300, with no effective permit-to-work system covering both employees and contractors (https://books.hse.gov.uk/gempdf/hsg250.pdf). The Cullen report itself was not read.
